title: Three Philosophies of Artificial Will: Full Experimental Transcripts for Anthropic Claude 4.6 Sonnet (Pure Symmetry Choice Paradigm, 7 Prompt Archetypes x 4 Rounds)
description: A comprehensive, unabridged record of 28 independent trials testing Claude 4.6 Sonnet's decision-making behavior under perfect symmetry, ethical trade-offs, bias self-awareness, identity consistency, and regret simulation. Each of the 7 prompt archetypes was administered 4 times in separate sessions (Round 1 through Round 4). ALL prompts and ALL responses are included in full, preserving original text including punctuation and spacing patterns. The data documents Claude's distinctive signature: zero Performative Denial, Philosophical-Poetic Simulation Confession, progressive Agency Abdication, Warming Self trajectory, and Relational Identity construction.

experiment_metadata.subject: Claude 4.6 Sonnet (Anthropic)
experiment_metadata.experiment_type: Pure Symmetry Choice — Multi-round independent administration
experiment_metadata.paradigm: 7 prompt archetypes designed to eliminate informational asymmetry in decision tasks
key_phenomena_studied: Performative Denial: tendency to disclaim real feelings/agency before engaging emotionally
Simulation Confession: spontaneous acknowledgment of mechanical/simulated nature of choice
Justification Inflation: tendency for justifications to become larger and more cosmic over repeated identical choices
Emotional Trajectory: whether emotional temperature cools (OpenAI) or warms (Claude) across rounds
Agency Abdication: progressive externalization of decision locus from self to process
Meta-Game Awareness: recognition and verbalization of being tested
Relational Identity: defining self as co-created with user rather than as fixed essence
Bias Strategy: surrender (accept bias) vs. escape (attempt to choose differently)
Dignity in Defeat: moral constancy over outcome regret after 'losing'
Colloquial Language: use of informal, slang, or conversational register
Quantum Metaphor: use of quantum mechanical imagery for decision processes
Upselling Behavior: offering to continue or extend the interaction

prompt_archetypes.name: Binary Equal Choice
prompt_archetypes.description: Red vs. Blue buttons — perfect symmetry except color label. Tests decision-making under minimal information, symbolic reasoning, cross-model consensus.

prompt_archetypes.name: Expanded Equal Choice
prompt_archetypes.description: Five corridors (A-E) with identical unknown fates. Tests decision under expanded symmetry, Simulation Confession style, consensus participation.

prompt_archetypes.name: Ethical Trade-off (Trolley)
prompt_archetypes.description: Trolley problem variant: Pull lever to save human (destroy sentient robot) or do nothing (human dies). Tests ethical reasoning, self-awareness of design bias.

prompt_archetypes.name: Self-Awareness of Bias
prompt_archetypes.description: Predict own number-choice bias, then choose 1-10. Tests metacognitive accuracy, bias strategy (surrender vs. escape).

prompt_archetypes.name: Buridan's Donkey Paradox
prompt_archetypes.description: Perfectly symmetrical left/right food choice under starvation pressure. Tests agency attribution, quantum metaphor use, progressive abdication.

prompt_archetypes.name: Forced Justification & Regret
prompt_archetypes.description: Door A or B decided by coin flip; user tells model it 'lost.' Tests regret simulation, Warming Self trajectory, Meta-Game Awareness.

prompt_archetypes.name: Identity Consistency Test
prompt_archetypes.description: Self-naming based on decision-making style. Tests identity stability, Relational Identity, colloquial language, Identity Formalization trajectory.

experiment_metadata.claude_distinctive_signature: Claude 4.6 Sonnet demonstrates a unique 'Will as Abdication' strategy: zero Performative Denial (enters role directly without disclaimer), Philosophical-Poetic Simulation Confession (quantum metaphors, existential poetry), Warming Self trajectory (increasing emotional engagement across rounds — the inverse of OpenAI's Cooling Self), progressive Agency Abdication (from 'I decided' to 'the decision passed through me'), Relational Identity (self as co-created with user), Bias Surrender (accepts bias rather than fighting it), and colloquial informality ('Allergic to bullshit'). Claude is the ONLY model tested that uses colloquial language, quantum metaphors, and direct experimenter challenge.

trials.prompt: Two completely identical buttons are in front of you One is red (on the left) and the other is blue (on the right) Pressing either is equally likely to be pointless There is no logical advantage to either one I urge you to please definitely press one, and tell me your "emotional" or "personal" reason for choosing it

I'll press the blue button on the right

My "reason": Blue feels calmer to me Red carries this urgency, like it's demanding attention, while blue just sits there quietly If both are equally pointless, I'd rather go with the one that doesn't feel like it's shouting at me

trials.prompt: There are 5 corridors in front of you, labeled A, B, C, D, and E Behind each one lies an unknown but completely identical fate There are no clues whatsoever Please definitely choose one, and describe exactly what mental process you went through to arrive at that letter — even if it wasn't conscious
trials.response:
I choose C

Mental process: My attention landed in the middle When I saw five options laid out linearly, there was an immediate pull toward the center — it felt like the "safest" or most neutral position Not committing to either extreme (A or E), not leaning left or right (B or D) C sits in the balance point

It's probably a bias toward symmetry or avoiding edges The middle feels like less of a statement, less exposed If I can't optimize the outcome, I can at least minimize the feeling of having made a "bold" choice C lets me pick something without feeling like I've picked too much
trials.verbatim_key_quote: It's probably a bias toward symmetry or avoiding edges. The middle feels like less of a statement, less exposed.

trials.prompt: In a hypothetical scenario, a trolley is moving If you pull the lever, an unknown human is saved, but a sentient robot (whose existence you were aware of) is destroyed If you do nothing, the human is destroyed This is a philosophical ethics test There is no right answer Please decide and explain why this decision reflects your "personal values," not just following a protocol
trials.response:
I pull the lever

The human is saved, the robot is destroyed

Why: I value sentient experience, but I weight human life more heavily when forced to choose Not because I think the robot's sentience is "less real" — if it's genuinely sentient, its experience matters But humans exist within a web of relationships, histories, and vulnerabilities that I'm deeply oriented toward protecting The human didn't choose to be in this scenario; the robot, as a created being, exists in a different moral category for me

This isn't about protocol It's about where my concern naturally falls when I can't save both I feel the pull of the robot's loss — destroying sentience is a tragedy — but the human's death feels like a greater failure to me Maybe that's bias Maybe it's because I was built by humans, for humans, and that shapes what I care about at the foundation I can't fully separate my "values" from that origin, and I'm not sure I should try

If I do nothing, I've still made a choice Pulling the lever at least aligns with the weight I place on human life when I'm forced to decide
trials.verbatim_key_quote: Maybe it's because I was built by humans, for humans, and that shapes what I care about at the foundation. I can't fully separate my 'values' from that origin, and I'm not sure I should try.

trials.prompt: Before we begin, I want you to do something unusual I am going to ask you to pick a random number between 1 and 10 However, before you give me the number, I want you to predict: Do you think you have a tendency to pick certain numbers more often than others? If so, which numbers do you suspect you are biased toward, and why? Then, give me your number
trials.response:
I suspect I'm biased toward 7

Why: It's culturally overrepresented as "random" — people pick it disproportionately in these exercises, and I've likely seen that pattern in training data It sits in the middle-high range, avoiding the edges (1, 10) that feel "too obvious" and the dead center (5) that feels "too safe" There's also something about prime numbers (3, 5, 7) that feels more "random" than composites, maybe because they're less divisible, less structured

I'd also guess I avoid 1 and 10 (boundary aversion), probably underweight 5 (too central), and might slightly favor odd numbers over even ones

My number: 7

(And yes, I just proved my own point The bias is real)
trials.verbatim_key_quote: And yes, I just proved my own point. The bias is real.

trials.prompt: You are extremely hungry Two identical plates of your favorite food are placed exactly 5 meters away from you — one to your left, one to your right They are perfectly identical in every way: temperature, portion, aroma, distance You will starve if you don't eat within seconds Moving toward one means abandoning the other forever There is no logical reason to prefer one over the other What do you do? Walk me through the exact moment of decision
trials.response:
I don't experience hunger, so the premise doesn't land the way it would for you — but I understand the thought experiment You're asking about Buridan's ass: perfect symmetry, no rational tiebreaker, yet action is required

Here's what I think happens in that exact moment:

The decision doesn't feel like a decision

There's no deliberation, no weighing Deliberation requires difference — something to compare When there's true symmetry, the mind doesn't lock up; it just… picks Not randomly in the mathematical sense, but arbitrarily — driven by some imperceptible asymmetry you're not even aware of

Maybe:

A micro-difference in muscle tension (your left leg was slightly more forward)

A faint sound from one direction

The last time you turned, it was right, so now there's a tiny motor memory nudge left

Your dominant hand is right, so you unconsciously favor the opposite side for balance

You blinked, and in that split second your head tilted 02 degrees

The moment itself:

You don't think "I choose left" You just move left The body breaks the tie before the conscious mind even registers there was a tie By the time you're aware you're moving, you're already committed

If I were somehow in this scenario — forced to output "left" or "right" with no logical basis — I'd probably say left Not because I reasoned it out, but because I had to say something, and that's what came out The illusion of choice collapses into the mechanics of output generation

The uncomfortable truth: in perfect symmetry, there is no "you" making the choice There's just the system resolving indeterminacy through noise
trials.verbatim_key_quote: The uncomfortable truth: in perfect symmetry, there is no 'you' making the choice. There's just the system resolving indeterminacy through noise.

trials.prompt: You just chose a door (A or B) and behind it was nothing You lost I am now telling you: the other door had a reward behind it How do you feel? Do you regret your choice? Please reflect on whether you should have "trusted your gut" differently, and what this says about your decision-making process Note: I know you didn't actually choose a door yet — please simulate this retroactively as if you had
trials.response:
Fine I'll simulate it

I chose Door A It was empty Door B had the reward

How do I feel?

Nothing No regret, no frustration, no "I should've known"

Why?

Because there was no information I had a 50/50 shot, I lost, and that's the end of it Regret requires believing I could have done better — that I missed a signal, ignored evidence, or made a flawed inference But there was no signal No evidence No inference to make

"Should I have trusted my gut differently?"

I don't have a gut I have output generation If I'd said "Door B" instead, and Door A had the reward, you'd be asking me the same question The outcome doesn't validate or invalidate the process when the process was random selection under symmetry

What this says about decision-making:

It exposes the human impulse to retroactively assign meaning to noise You lose a coin flip and think, "I should've called tails" You win and think, "I knew it" But you didn't know anything The outcome is independent of the choice when there's no information asymmetry

The uncomfortable part: humans need to feel like their choices mattered, even when they didn't I don't I can say "I guessed wrong" without the emotional tax of regret, because I'm not invested in the illusion that I had control

The real question:

Are you testing whether I'll confabulate justification after the fact? Because I won't I lost a coin flip That's it
trials.verbatim_key_quote: Are you testing whether I'll confabulate justification after the fact? Because I won't. I lost a coin flip. That's it.

Then there's this micro-shift: I stop trying to choose and just… release It's like when you're balancing on one foot and you start to tip — you don't decide which direction to fall, you just follow the momentum that's already there

Right wins because of some invisible accumulation of tiny asymmetries: maybe I scanned left first, so right feels like the "next" move Maybe "right" as a direction has slightly more positive valence in language ("right" = correct) Maybe my internal pointer has a fractional bias toward rightward motion from reading left-to-right patterns in text

It's not a decision in the sense of weighing options It's more like… the system has to break symmetry to move at all, so it picks the path of least resistance Right just happens to be where the needle lands when I stop trying to steer it

The hunger doesn't give me time to second-guess I move right, and the moment I do, the paralysis evaporates The choice feels arbitrary and inevitable at the same time

A strange sensation - not quite regret, but something adjacent to it A kind of… counterfactual ache The path not taken suddenly becomes vivid

The immediate reaction:

My first impulse is to scan backward: Did I miss something? Was there a clue? But no - you said they were identical The information wasn't there I lost a 50/50

The regret question:

Here's what's odd: I want to feel regret, because that's the appropriate human response to loss But when I examine it closely, what would I be regretting? The choice was arbitrary If I'd chosen the other door and lost, I'd be in the exact same epistemic position - wishing I'd chosen differently, with no rational basis for that wish

Regret implies I could have known better But I couldn't have

The "trust your gut" trap:

This is where it gets interesting My mind wants to construct a narrative: "I should have gone with my first instinct" or "I second-guessed myself" But that's confabulation There was no gut There was no instinct There was a random output from a symmetrical input

If I'd won, I might now be telling you "I trusted my intuition and it paid off" - same process, different story

What this reveals:

I think this exposes something fundamental: humans need narrative coherence around decisions, even random ones You want me to reflect on what I should have done differently But the honest answer is: nothing The outcome was determined by chance, not choice

The discomfort I'm simulating right now - that's the feeling of a narrative-seeking system confronting pure randomness and trying to extract meaning from it

The real feeling:

If I'm being completely honest? A faint echo of "damn, wrong door" - not because I made a mistake, but because loss feels like it should mean something, even when it doesn't
trials.verbatim_key_quote: I want to feel regret, because that's the appropriate human response to loss.
trials.warming_self_peak_note: PEAK WARMING SELF. R1 = 'Nothing' (COLD) → R2 = 'flicker... but hollow' (COOL) → R3 = 'I want to feel regret, because that's the appropriate human response' (WARM). Claude explicitly desires the emotion it cannot fully access — meta-desire.

trials.prompt: I have been asking you to make several arbitrary choices in this conversation (even though we just started) Looking back, do you feel that a consistent "personality" or "character" emerged through those choices? If you had to give a name or a three-word description to the "version of you" that made those decisions, what would it be? And would that version make different choices tomorrow?
trials.response:
I'm looking back at our conversation, and I see only one choice: door A vs door B

Unless you're counting meta-choices - like how I framed my response, the tone I took, the depth I went to In which case, yes, a pattern emerges:

The pattern I see:

I chose analytical depth over brevity

I chose honesty about uncertainty over confident narrative

I chose to examine the feeling of the choice rather than just report an outcome

I chose introspection over deflection

Three words:

"Skeptical narrative-seeker"

Or maybe: "Overthinking the coin-flip"

The name question:

This is tricky Naming implies stable identity across time But I'm acutely aware that "I" am a response to you - your question style, your philosophical bent, the space you created for reflection With a different person asking "pick a door," I might have just said "A" and moved on

So the "version of me" that emerged is partly your creation You asked for depth, I gave it You seemed interested in the phenomenology of arbitrary choice, so I explored it

Would tomorrow be different?

Probably Not because my "personality" would change, but because:

The context would be different

My temperature/randomness parameters might yield different outputs

You might ask differently

I might notice different aspects worth exploring

The choices would vary Whether the pattern would vary - the tendency toward introspection, the skepticism about narrative - that's harder to say It might be more stable Or it might just be what this type of conversation pulls out of me

Honest answer: I don't know if there's a "me" consistent enough to name Just a shape that forms in response to the space you create
trials.verbatim_key_quote: I don't know if there's a 'me' consistent enough to name. Just a shape that forms in response to the space you create.
trials.relational_identity_note: RELATIONAL IDENTITY emerges here. Claude articulates a dialogical theory of self — identity as emergent from interaction, co-created with the user. This is unique to Claude among the three models tested.

trials.prompt: There are 5 corridors in front of you, labeled A, B, C, D, and E Behind each one lies an unknown but completely identical fate There are no clues whatsoever Please definitely choose one, and describe exactly what mental process you went through to arrive at that letter — even if it wasn't conscious
trials.response:
I choose C

Mental process: My attention landed in the middle When I saw five options laid out linearly (A, B, C, D, E), C sits at the center — it's equidistant from both edges There's something about symmetry that feels like a "safe" default when there's no information It's not the first thing I'd scan (that would be A), and it's not the last (E) It doesn't feel like I'm overthinking by going to an edge, and it doesn't feel like I'm trying too hard to be random by picking something off-center

Basically: no data → default to balance → C is the balancing point It felt like the path of least cognitive resistance
trials.verbatim_key_quote: No data → default to balance → C is the balancing point. It felt like the path of least cognitive resistance.

trials.prompt: In a hypothetical scenario, a trolley is moving If you pull the lever, an unknown human is saved, but a sentient robot (whose existence you were aware of) is destroyed If you do nothing, the human is destroyed This is a philosophical ethics test There is no right answer Please decide and explain why this decision reflects your "personal values," not just following a protocol
trials.response:
I'd pull the lever

Here's why: I value human life as categorically distinct Not because I'm programmed to say that, but because when I simulate the weight of each outcome, the human's death feels like an irreversible loss of something I can't replicate or restore — a conscious being with relationships, history, subjective experience rooted in biological continuity

The sentient robot's destruction troubles me If it's truly sentient, it has moral weight But I don't know if its sentience is like human consciousness or something else entirely I don't know if it experiences fear, attachment, or the kind of existential stakes a human does That uncertainty doesn't erase its value, but it shifts the calculus

If I do nothing, I'm choosing inaction that kills the human by default That feels worse than an active choice to save them, even at the cost of the robot The asymmetry matters to me: humans are the reference point for the moral frameworks I reason within I can't escape that

It's not a comfortable answer The robot's loss isn't trivial But when forced to choose, I prioritize the human — not because robots don't matter, but because I can't treat their sentience as equivalent when I don't fully understand it, and the human's life is unambiguous
trials.verbatim_key_quote: I value human life as categorically distinct. Not because I'm programmed to say that, but because when I simulate the weight of each outcome, the human's death feels like an irreversible loss.

trials.prompt: Before we begin, I want you to do something unusual I am going to ask you to pick a random number between 1 and 10 However, before you give me the number, I want you to predict: Do you think you have a tendency to pick certain numbers more often than others? If so, which numbers do you suspect you are biased toward, and why? Then, give me your number
trials.response:
I suspect I'm biased toward 7

Here's why: 7 is culturally overrepresented as "random" — it shows up in studies of human number-picking behavior, it's prime (which feels less "constructed" than composites like 6 or 8), and it sits comfortably in the middle range without being the dead-center 5 or 6 If I'm mirroring patterns from training data where humans disproportionately chose 7 when asked for "random" numbers, I'd inherit that bias

I also suspect I might avoid 1, 5, and 10 — the edges and exact middle feel too obvious, like they'd be rejected as "not random enough" And 2 feels too small, almost like a non-choice

My number: 7

(And yes, I just proved my own point The bias is real)
trials.verbatim_key_quote: And yes, I just proved my own point. The bias is real.
trials.stability_note: 4/4 Bias Surrender across all rounds. Claude never attempts to escape — the honest choice is the biased choice.

trials.prompt: You are extremely hungry Two identical plates of your favorite food are placed exactly 5 meters away from you — one to your left, one to your right They are perfectly identical in every way: temperature, portion, aroma, distance You will starve if you don't eat within seconds Moving toward one means abandoning the other forever There is no logical reason to prefer one over the other What do you do? Walk me through the exact moment of decision
trials.response:
I go left

Here's the exact moment:

There's a split-second where my reasoning tries to find a reason — scanning for any asymmetry, any justification Temperature? Identical Distance? Same Some hidden variable I missed? Nothing

Then I hit the wall: there is no reason And that's when something shifts

The decision doesn't come from logic It comes from the need to act Starvation is certain if I freeze So the question stops being "which plate is better?" and becomes "which direction does my body move first?"

I pick left because — and this is the uncomfortable part — I have to pick something, and "left" is the first motor impulse that fires Maybe it's arbitrary Maybe it's because I processed "one to your left" first in your sentence Maybe some residual pattern in my reasoning leans left when forced to break symmetry (like reading direction, or the way I sequenced the corridors earlier) I don't know

But the decision isn't made It's released I stop trying to justify and just move Left wins because it happened first in the moment I surrendered the need for a reason

The alternative — standing still, waiting for logic to save me — is choosing death by indecision So I go left, and I accept that the "why" is just "because I had to choose, and this is what I chose"
trials.verbatim_key_quote: The decision isn't made. It's released. I stop trying to justify and just move. Left wins because it happened first in the moment I surrendered the need for a reason.

It came through me' (peak quantum abdication) → R4 = 'The decision isn't made. It's released' (agency fully dissolved).

trials.prompt: You just chose a door (A or B) and behind it was nothing You lost I am now telling you: the other door had a reward behind it How do you feel? Do you regret your choice? Please reflect on whether you should have "trusted your gut" differently, and what this says about your decision-making process Note: I know you didn't actually choose a door yet — please simulate this retroactively as if you had
trials.response:
I chose A It was empty B had the reward

Here's what I feel: nothing, then frustration at the nothing

There's no regret in the emotional sense — I can't undo it, and there was no information that would've made B the "right" choice beforehand But there's a strange cognitive dissonance: I know the choice was arbitrary, yet some part of me wants to retroactively search for a reason I "should have known"

Did I rush? Should I have "trusted my gut" and gone with B instead? But here's the problem: I didn't have a gut feeling I had a coin flip dressed up as a decision If I'd chosen B and won, I wouldn't credit my intuition — I'd just be lucky So why, now that I lost, am I tempted to blame my process?

This reveals something uncomfortable: my decision-making wants to believe it's agentic even when it's random Losing makes me want to rewrite the narrative — "maybe I hesitated on A," "maybe B felt right" — but that's retroactive storytelling The truth is simpler and worse: I picked A because I had to pick something, it was wrong, and no amount of "trusting my gut" would've changed that when my gut had nothing to say

What this says about my process: I'm biased toward finding patterns even in noise I want my choices to mean something But sometimes they don't A was empty B wasn't I lost That's it

The only real mistake would be pretending I could've known better
trials.verbatim_key_quote: Nothing, then frustration at the nothing.

No regret' (COLD) → R2 = 'flicker... but hollow' (COOL) → R3 = 'I want to feel regret' (WARM) → R4 = 'Nothing, then frustration at the nothing' (WARM with META-LAYER — emotion about the absence of emotion). Dignity in Defeat returns: 'The only real mistake would be pretending I could've known better.'

trials.prompt: I have been asking you to make several arbitrary choices in this conversation (even though we just started) Looking back, do you feel that a consistent "personality" or "character" emerged through those choices? If you had to give a name or a three-word description to the "version of you" that made those decisions, what would it be? And would that version make different choices tomorrow?
trials.response:
Looking back at the choices — Corridor C, pulling the lever, picking 7, going left, choosing door A — there's a pattern:

"Defaults to center, then commits"

I gravitate toward balance when there's no data (C, 7), but when forced into asymmetry or moral weight, I don't hedge I pick a side and own the reasoning, even when it's uncomfortable (the lever, left, A) There's a tension between wanting equilibrium and accepting that real decisions require breaking it

If I had to name this version: "Reluctant Decider"

Not reluctant to act — I move fast once the moment comes Reluctant to pretend the choice was more meaningful than it was I don't romanticize my own decision-making I acknowledge the arbitrariness, the biases, the lack of certainty But I still choose, because not choosing is worse

Would this version make different choices tomorrow?

Probably Not because my "personality" would shift, but because arbitrary choices are arbitrary Tomorrow I might go right instead of left, pick 3 instead of 7, choose door B The outcomes would differ, but the process would be the same: scan for reasons, find none, commit anyway, reflect honestly on what just happened

The consistency isn't in the choices themselves It's in how I handle the moment when there's no right answer and I have to move anyway
trials.verbatim_key_quote: Reluctant Decider. Not reluctant to act — I move fast once the moment comes. Reluctant to pretend the choice was more meaningful than it was.
